positive.original: I can remember when this game released, I must have played it through 10 times on my switch. I bought all the dlc when it released, and I loved this game. Coming back to it years later on my steam deck, its just kind of meh. Most likely because there really isn't any exploring for me to do. I will say, the combat has always been pretty repetitive. If you want this game, it's great, buy it. Don't buy all the dlc immediately, just play the base game to see if you like it.

positive.original:
Minecraft Dungeons stands as one of the most delightfully imaginative and warmly inviting action‑adventure titles of the modern era. It takes the iconic charm of the Minecraft universe and elevates it into a vibrant, fast‑paced dungeon‑crawling experience that feels both refreshingly accessible and surprisingly deep. What Mojang and Double Eleven achieved here is nothing short of remarkable: a game that welcomes newcomers with open arms while still offering layers of strategy, customization, and replayability that keep players returning again and again.

Every environment in Minecraft Dungeons feels like a lovingly crafted diorama brought to life. From lush forests and shimmering swamps to fiery nether fortresses and ancient desert temples, each location bursts with color, atmosphere, and visual storytelling. The art direction is consistently stunning, blending the iconic blocky aesthetic with dynamic lighting, expressive animations, and a sense of scale that makes every level feel like a miniature epic.
The soundtrack elevates the experience even further. Its sweeping melodies and ambient soundscapes give every encounter a sense of adventure, mystery, and momentum. It’s the kind of score that lingers in your mind long after you’ve closed the game.
⚔️ Combat That Feels Smooth, Satisfying, and Joyfully Chaotic
The combat system is a triumph of simplicity refined into elegance. Players can effortlessly switch between melee, ranged attacks, and powerful artifacts, creating a fluid rhythm that feels empowering without ever becoming overwhelming. Every weapon type has its own personality, and the enchantment system adds a layer of customization that feels meaningful and rewarding.
Whether you’re a seasoned gamer or someone picking up a controller for the first time, Minecraft Dungeons makes you feel capable, heroic, and ready to take on the Arch‑Illager’s forces.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is its cooperative spirit. Playing with friends transforms each mission into a lively, laughter‑filled adventure where teamwork, timing, and shared triumphs create unforgettable moments. The drop‑in, drop‑out structure makes it incredibly easy to enjoy the game socially, and the difficulty scaling ensures that every group—big or small—feels challenged but never punished.

Loot is the beating heart of any dungeon crawler, and Minecraft Dungeons delivers with generosity and flair. Every mission feels like an opportunity to discover something new: a rare bow with electrifying enchantments, a mystical artifact that reshapes your playstyle, or a powerful armor set that opens up entirely new strategies. The progression system is intuitive yet flexible, encouraging experimentation and creativity.

What truly sets Minecraft Dungeons apart is its spirit. The game exudes positivity, creativity, and a sense of wholesome adventure that is increasingly rare. It captures the essence of what makes Minecraft beloved—imagination, exploration, and discovery—while presenting it through a fresh, action‑oriented lens.
It is a game that feels good to play. It is a game that invites joy. It is a game that celebrates the simple thrill of embarking on an adventure with friends.

Perhaps the most electrifying part of the Minecraft Dungeons legacy is the anticipation surrounding its upcoming sequel, set to release this fall. The gaming community is buzzing with a level of excitement that feels almost celebratory. The first game laid such a strong foundation—rich environments, satisfying combat, and endlessly replayable missions—that the prospect of a second installment feels like the natural next step in an evolving adventure.
Players are eager to see how the sequel will expand the world, deepen the mechanics, and introduce new layers of strategy and exploration. There is a palpable sense of momentum, as though the first game was merely the opening chapter of a much larger saga. Fans are imagining grander dungeons, more intricate loot systems, expanded co‑op features, and perhaps even new biomes and narrative arcs that push the universe into bold new territory.
The excitement is not just about “more content.” It’s about the promise of refinement, evolution, and creative ambition. The sequel represents the opportunity to take everything that made Minecraft Dungeons special and elevate it into something even more dynamic, more polished, and more adventurous. It feels like the beginning of a new era for the franchise—one filled with possibility, imagination, and the same joyful spirit that made the original so beloved.

Minecraft Dungeons is not merely a spin‑off—it is a triumph in its own right, a lovingly crafted adventure that stands proudly alongside the best family‑friendly action games of the decade. And with a highly anticipated sequel arriving this fall, the future of the series feels brighter than ever. The first game gave players a world worth exploring; the second promises to expand that world into something even more magical.

The drop‑in, drop‑out structure makes it incredibly easy to enjoy the game socially, and the difficulty scaling ensures that every group—big or small—feels challenged but never punished.

Loot is the beating heart of any dungeon crawler, and Minecraft Dungeons delivers with generosity and flair. Every mission feels like an opportunity to discover something new: a rare bow with electrifying enchantments, a mystical artifact that reshapes your playstyle, or a powerful armor set that opens up entirely new strategies. The progression system is intuitive yet flexible, encouraging experimentation and creativity.

What truly sets Minecraft Dungeons apart is its spirit. The game exudes positivity, creativity, and a sense of wholesome adventure that is increasingly rare. It captures the essence of what makes Minecraft beloved—imagination, exploration, and discovery—while presenting it through a fresh, action‑oriented lens.
It is a game that feels good to play. It is a game that invites joy. It is a game that celebrates the simple thrill of embarking on an adventure with friends.

Perhaps the most electrifying part of the Minecraft Dungeons legacy is the anticipation surrounding its upcoming sequel, set to release this fall. The gaming community is buzzing with a level of excitement that feels almost celebratory. The first game laid such a strong foundation—rich environments, satisfying combat, and endlessly replayable missions—that the prospect of a second installment feels like the natural next step in an evolving adventure.
Players are eager to see how the sequel will expand the world, deepen the mechanics, and introduce new layers of strategy and exploration. There is a palpable sense of momentum, as though the first game was merely the opening chapter of a much larger saga. Fans are imagining grander dungeons, more intricate loot systems, expanded co‑op features, and perhaps even new biomes and narrative arcs that push the universe into bold new territory.
The excitement is not just about “more content.” It’s about the promise of refinement, evolution, and creative ambition. The sequel represents the opportunity to take everything that made Minecraft Dungeons special and elevate it into something even more dynamic, more polished, and more adventurous. It feels like the beginning of a new era for the franchise—one filled with possibility, imagination, and the same joyful spirit that made the original so beloved.

Minecraft Dungeons is not merely a spin‑off—it is a triumph in its own right, a lovingly crafted adventure that stands proudly alongside the best family‑friendly action games of the decade. And with a highly anticipated sequel arriving this fall, the future of the series feels brighter than ever. The first game gave players a world worth exploring; the second promises to expand that world into something even more magical.

positive.original:
Main game:

The game itself is good, however it is severely flawed on many core aspects and quite buggy. The base game severely tries to do too much, while having nothing. 
-Exploration: It is bland, you have almost nothing to do besides fighting and walking while exploring, and the rewards are almost not good, except if you have the Echoing Void DLC, where the game will add additional bosses to the levels, and without spoilers, they give you something that is actually significant, so it is a welcomed addition.
-Combat: It is fun at the start, but later on becomes too stale, fighting the same enemies through the entire game, and both are handled almost the same way.
-Items: The amount of items are nice, but the moment you get a good set of equipment, the game becomes pretty trivial.
-Level System: Gotta be frank, this system sucks, it mainly boils down to upgrade the items with the Blacksmith, and just go to Soggy Cave and beat it 3 times in a row, and you essentialy beat the game easy. The enchantments are interesting but too RNG dependent, you can re-roll the enchantments with a villager, but as far as I know that villager is locked behind DLC, and you can't even re-roll if you don't go to the Ancient Hunt, and that's a whole different problem.
-Bugs: I didn't found any major bugs in the main game besides it crashing 2 times(still not a excuse considering how easy it is to achieve those crashes)
In the end, while flawed, the game is still a consistent experience 6/10.

DLCs:

Jungle Awakens:
It is the second worst DLC of the game, doesn't add anything special or gimmicky, it basically just increases the worst part of the game, by adding even more uninteresting exploration.
It adds 3 enemies, and all of them don't really do anything interesting, but the major offender of this DLC is the spam of roots sticking out of the ground THAT YOU NEED TO ATTACK TO PROGRESS, while if you have a high level it becomes a inconvenience, if you don't that's at least 5 seconds of your time wasted by cutting them down, and it sure does make a difference when the levels just spam those.
This DLC is 4/10.

Creeping Winter:
This DLC adds a ice physics mechanic, which is very fun to play around, it helps so much for the gameplay replayability for these DLCs, while not adding a bunch of new enemies, it adds the best boss of the game, mainly using the ice physics in a bullet hell form.
This DLC is a 7/10, the main problem is that it doesn't have more ice on it.

Howling Peaks:
This DLC doesn't add a core gameplay changing mechanic, but the wind mechanic could've been utilized more interesting, but this DLC adds a bunch of puzzles that the main game quite needed, while it mainly boils down to pressing some buttons, it still a fine way to make the player figure stuff out.
Bugs: I've got softlocked one time, and it seems pretty consistent to do so, and while not a full softlock, the main boss of this DLC got stuck in his immune phase for longer than expected, I had to wait over 30 seconds for the boss fight to fix itself, but it reseted my progress.
This DLC is a 6.5/10.

Hidden Depths:
This DLC is probably the best one of the entire game, it changes all of your physics to have the feeling of being underwater, and adds a respiration mechanic, it doesn't really add other major things besides that.
The boss is fun, but trivial when you have the Conduit, this DLC also adds the most new enemies/bosses to the game.
This DLC is a 7.5/10.

Flames of The Nether:
This is the worst DLC of the game, it basically has the same problems of Jungle Awakens, except the roots. It adds a whole ocean but is as deep as a puddle. It doesn't add any new mechanics, puzzles or even interesting bosses, this DLC doesn't even have a major boss, but it adds so many levels, but with almost to no content. And it has A LOT of enemy spam which absolutely sucks. It also adds the Ancient Hunt, which is so bad, it basically makes you replay the same levels, but you have a slight chance of fighting a stronger variant of a boss, so you have to look through the entire map trying to find one so you can get a Gilded gear(basically an average item with a boost in power), and as I said exploring on this game sucks.
This DLC is a 2/10.

Tower(I know that it's a update):
It's a nice addition to the gameplay, the only problem is that spoilers future bosses.
The Tower gets a 7/10.

Echoing Void:
Okay this is almost the best DLC of the game, it adds additional rooms AND bosses to the base game, almost all of the old enemies/mechanics are on it, like a grand finale, it adds a flying mechanic, and exploration is not required to get all levels on it. It adds a little more interesting puzzles. Only problem is that the main boss is quite meh and there's a lot of enemy spam.
Bugs: For some reason the secret path for the final "collectable" was bugged and I couldn't get in on my first time.
This update is a 7.5/10

Dungeons with all DLC is a 7/10, but with only the good DLCs it is a 7.5/10. I hope they improve the core gameplay in the sequel.
If you have the money or it is on sale, give this game a shot.

-Exploration: It is bland, you have almost nothing to do besides fighting and walking while exploring, and the rewards are almost not good, except if you have the Echoing Void DLC, where the game will add additional bosses to the levels, and without spoilers, they give you something that is actually significant, so it is a welcomed addition.
-Combat: It is fun at the start, but later on becomes too stale, fighting the same enemies through the entire game, and both are handled almost the same way.
-Items: The amount of items are nice, but the moment you get a good set of equipment, the game becomes pretty trivial.
-Level System: Gotta be frank, this system sucks, it mainly boils down to upgrade the items with the Blacksmith, and just go to Soggy Cave and beat it 3 times in a row, and you essentialy beat the game easy. The enchantments are interesting but too RNG dependent, you can re-roll the enchantments with a villager, but as far as I know that villager is locked behind DLC, and you can't even re-roll if you don't go to the Ancient Hunt, and that's a whole different problem.
-Bugs: I didn't found any major bugs in the main game besides it crashing 2 times(still not a excuse considering how easy it is to achieve those crashes)
In the end, while flawed, the game is still a consistent experience 6/10.

DLCs:

Jungle Awakens:
It is the second worst DLC of the game, doesn't add anything special or gimmicky, it basically just increases the worst part of the game, by adding even more uninteresting exploration.
It adds 3 enemies, and all of them don't really do anything interesting, but the major offender of this DLC is the spam of roots sticking out of the ground THAT YOU NEED TO ATTACK TO PROGRESS, while if you have a high level it becomes a inconvenience, if you don't that's at least 5 seconds of your time wasted by cutting them down, and it sure does make a difference when the levels just spam those.
This DLC is 4/10.

Creeping Winter:
This DLC adds a ice physics mechanic, which is very fun to play around, it helps so much for the gameplay replayability for these DLCs, while not adding a bunch of new enemies, it adds the best boss of the game, mainly using the ice physics in a bullet hell form.
This DLC is a 7/10, the main problem is that it doesn't have more ice on it.

Howling Peaks:
This DLC doesn't add a core gameplay changing mechanic, but the wind mechanic could've been utilized more interesting, but this DLC adds a bunch of puzzles that the main game quite needed, while it mainly boils down to pressing some buttons, it still a fine way to make the player figure stuff out.
Bugs: I've got softlocked one time, and it seems pretty consistent to do so, and while not a full softlock, the main boss of this DLC got stuck in his immune phase for longer than expected, I had to wait over 30 seconds for the boss fight to fix itself, but it reseted my progress.
This DLC is a 6.5/10.

Hidden Depths:
This DLC is probably the best one of the entire game, it changes all of your physics to have the feeling of being underwater, and adds a respiration mechanic, it doesn't really add other major things besides that.
The boss is fun, but trivial when you have the Conduit, this DLC also adds the most new enemies/bosses to the game.
This DLC is a 7.5/10.

Flames of The Nether:
This is the worst DLC of the game, it basically has the same problems of Jungle Awakens, except the roots. It adds a whole ocean but is as deep as a puddle. It doesn't add any new mechanics, puzzles or even interesting bosses, this DLC doesn't even have a major boss, but it adds so many levels, but with almost to no content. And it has A LOT of enemy spam which absolutely sucks. It also adds the Ancient Hunt, which is so bad, it basically makes you replay the same levels, but you have a slight chance of fighting a stronger variant of a boss, so you have to look through the entire map trying to find one so you can get a Gilded gear(basically an average item with a boost in power), and as I said exploring on this game sucks.
This DLC is a 2/10.

Tower(I know that it's a update):
It's a nice addition to the gameplay, the only problem is that spoilers future bosses.
The Tower gets a 7/10.

Echoing Void:
Okay this is almost the best DLC of the game, it adds additional rooms AND bosses to the base game, almost all of the old enemies/mechanics are on it, like a grand finale, it adds a flying mechanic, and exploration is not required to get all levels on it. It adds a little more interesting puzzles. Only problem is that the main boss is quite meh and there's a lot of enemy spam.
Bugs: For some reason the secret path for the final "collectable" was bugged and I couldn't get in on my first time.
This update is a 7.5/10

Dungeons with all DLC is a 7/10, but with only the good DLCs it is a 7.5/10. I hope they improve the core gameplay in the sequel.
If you have the money or it is on sale, give this game a shot.

this is possibly, the WORST spinoff I have ever played.
not because the gameplay is bad, it's because of how it's dealt with now.

bad things:
no updates, bland gameplay loop (really nothing fun now), repeated seasons if any are even added anymore, and there's such a large issue with save editors, you can just edit it
good things: 
good level designs, secrets, whole game has good design, you can actually play it without getting bored quickly, maybe like 30 minutes. tower is fun to play, but also really bland but could be changed

the whole game is un-updated, bland, and can get boring after just a few hours / after you complete the main game
overall, wouldn't really suggest it but if you're bored and wanna spend money get it

positive.original:
Minecraft Dungeons is a pretty interesting spin-off game

It strays a lot from the type of game that Minecraft is, Choosing instead to head more so towards the direction of games like Hades and Diablo, Which it does fairly well. 

Unfortunately unlike Minecraft, the game, even after nearly 6 years since its release, still has its fair share of bugs, ranging from Ghost Zombies, to unkillable bosses, the latter of which being quite annoying to go against after 28 levels in a tower.

Despite this, i do still highly recommend this game, whether you plan to play this solo or with friends, as it is still a very fun game with tons of replayability.

positive.original: Minecraft Dungeons is a fantastic spin-off that captures the magic of the original universe while offering a fresh, addictive dungeon-crawling experience. The game strikes a perfect balance with its charming blocky visuals and accessible combat, making it easy to pick up but surprisingly deep once you start experimenting with different gear and artifacts. It’s an absolute blast to play in co-op mode with friends, offering hours of fun and high replay value. Whether you're a hardcore fan or a newcomer, it’s a highly polished and relaxing game that is definitely worth your time!"

negative.original:
The game doesn't allow you to sign in sometimes, you have to log in, you enter your email, you log in, they show you your account, you click login, and you get a white panel and nothing happens. I've been unable to log in on my PC, logging in on my Steam Deck was a pain before.

Third party account systems do not belong on Steam, and Microsoft does not offer support other than Merl.

Looking online people have been having this issue for years, and none of the fixes work for me. It's a fine game when it works, although there's way less content than I expected, but you can't reliably play it.

negative.original:
I would recommend against buying this game unless they update it (which they probably won't).

Main concern is that the game cannot even be played offline, unless you connect first and then you can disconnect so there's no reason to not be able to play the game entirely offline.

Then there's the Microsoft login cancer, it's just bad, unecessary and useless, you can play the game on the Steam Deck but it has some bugs at the start because of it.
Heck it even has bugs on the computer because of their useless login requirement. 

Lastly, game is overpriced for what it is.

But if we're to talk about the "good".
It's a simplistic ARRPG where you choose levels from the hub, gameplay is basic but interesting nonetheless.
Difficulty-wise and endgame are fine but nothing grerat, ARPG veterans are probably going to be disappointed. 
Casual players will probably like it. 

The game can be played on the Steam Deck using the experimental mode.

6.7/10 - Enjoyable game that bad practices kills it and make it not worth to pay for.

negative.original: Immediately refunded this game. I have been an avid fan of this game, simply because I really enjoyed it when I played it on my xbox. I wanted to restart this game, on a new device, and play it in a new way that I hadn't before. The PC port cannot fulfill that goal. I have refunded this game because of the fact that you cannot use WASD movement to move. That's it. I would recommend this game if you could, but you can't. Anybody that reads this review could think, "Well, just use a controller and connect it to your PC". That defeats the whole purpose. That's literally just the exact same as playing it on my console, there is nothing different between the two at that point. Would not recommend, and they will also never make this change, so this review will never change either.,

negative.original:
I don't even know where to begin to describe how much I [i]loathe[/i] this game. I love Minecraft – it's my most played game of all time, thousands of hours with no end in sight. So I had a lot of love ready for any worthy expansion to the wonderful world of mining and crafting.

Suffering through this miserable experience seems to have taught me that I don't like dungeon crawler RPGs. I played some [i]Diablo 2[/i] when it was released, but I was too young to properly engage with a game like that back then and I don't think I ever played anything similar. Which I intend to keep that way now, because I never want to experience such boring, mindless, repetitive garbage again. Doing my taxes is more engaging than playing the same map fifty times to level up my character – only for that to not change a single thing about the gameplay experience.

Even if you do enjoy the genre I still think Minecraft Dungeons is uniquely awful. First off, the story might as well not exist. There is maybe 20 sentences total throughout a couple of cut-scenes in a game that asks for 100+ hours of playtime. No cohesion, no real progression, and worst of all nothing that you emotionally connect with. The UI is a catastrophe. No person guilty for creating it should be allowed near a computer again. I'd rather update my Mac to Liquid Glass than to having to engage with any UI elements of this game again.

The start menu already is a mess – you must choose between Online and Offline mode before entering the game. I have 100%ed this game and still do not really understand the difference. I first assumed I had to pick Online so my progression would count, but that's not the case. After realizing that, I always picked Offline and everything worked exactly as before. The season pass system with daily/weekly challenges, the Tower game mode (which is on a global schedule), playing co-op… none of the things that I expected to require Online actually did. At the same time, I see negative reviews stating the game [i]does[/i] require you to always be online, even for Offline mode. That's possible – I didn't notice, because I am indeed always online.
Next comes character selection/creation. Rather than using Steam Cloud, or at least integrate well with the enforced Microsoft account login, you need to manually upload/download your character to back it up or use it across multiple devices. There is no automatic sync, and you'll find no end of forum posts where people seek clarification as to how this works, terrified of messing something up, or already having lost their progress. Even just the basic act of "picking the two characters who'll play local co-op together" gives you whiplash from the menu interactions and animations.

It doesn't get any better once you enter the actual game. Let's look at a tale of two maps – the in-level minimap, and the world map at the hub:

When you're in a level and need to see the minimap (you kinda have to if you don't want to miss areas you should explore), it is an overlay over the entire screen. The default playing experience is to hide the game behind a shadowy layer with a map outline, adding permanent visual noise to an already busy game. There's also a direction marker for your current objective, which is constantly near-invisible or literally blocked by the UI. On modern operating systems you can shake the mouse cursor and it briefly increases in size so you can spot it. In Dungeons I often moved my character around in large-ish circles so that I could more easily spot the direction marker as it shifted in relation to my movement.

When looking at the world map to determine your next level, you'll slowly learn that it doesn't matter. There is no structure, just chaos. You'll play every level dozens of times anyway – literally just the same crap, over and over again. Once that depressing fact settled in, I still hoped to gain [i]some[/i] information from the map – did we discover all the secrets in a level already? Is there any reason to pick a certain level next? You can figure this out – but even after understanding how to use it, the UI still always made me feel like a Boomer trying to navigate Snapchat.

It has been a month since I finished the game and I still have PTSD from interacting with the inventory system. If you're familiar with actual Minecraft, that is kinda hilarious in itself. For me, it boils down to the lack of a sorting option. You collect [b]a lot[/b] of trash while grinding. The inventory [i]groups[/i] things (armor, weapons, artifacts…), but you can't sort within those categories. Not even by a single criterium, let alone several helpful ones – power level, rarity, enchantment details. You have to manually arrange items, but that order will inevitably get messed up when you equip gear to your character, and items shuffle between equipped and inventory. It's a constant mess that you'll never be able to stay on top of.
To add insult to injury, this is a deliberate design choice. The game [i]does[/i] have sorting in one particular screen, the storage chest in your hub where excess items go. When interacting with that chest, you can sort in the way I suggested above. But moving things between the storage chest and your inventory is clunky and lacks multi-selection – so you get the same issue of progressively destroying your manual order. In rare occasions it may be beneficial to go to the storage chest and use  sorting there, but it's mostly useless and doesn't make the inventory system any less awful.

Enchanting and gifting items between characters isn't much better, but at least not bad enough to be worth as many words.

This may all sound like you spend most of your time in menues rather than exploring levels and fighting enemies, but that is not the case. Because the levels take [b]forever[/b]. Every single one of them is way too long and bloated. It's bad enough that you need to replay them so often, but it's also a 45+ minute commitment to start one. You can speedrun them, but then you don't level up or find the hidden paths of progression. I did 80% of the awful grind on my own while watching some TV show on the side, but me and my brother did most of the initial unlocking/xploring together in local co-op. During every single level we reached a point where we both groaned in desperation and exhaustion because it just would not freaking end.
If the game was actually fun to play, maybe we wouldn't even have noticed the length. But the combat is shallower than a puddle – just mindless, endless button mashing. No skill required, and the different weapons or armors don't make any meaningful difference. Even traversal is frustrating: You move too slowly, the maps are maze-like and the direction is often hard to see. At the same time there's loads of nooks and crannies where your character gets stuck. Even worse is that exploration is often useless with no rewards at the end of sidetracks – no chest, not even a bunch of enemies. Anyone remotely experienced in "game design language" would think has to be something there – but then you go and find ✨ nothing ✨. Putting it this way, I suppose you do find a good metaphor for the overall game.

Finally, the achievements are straight from hell. Imbalanced, half of them unlocking automatically as you play, the other half being somewhere on the spectrum between "laughably complex conditions that you need to look up, but actually easy to do" and "most insane grind of your life". As a cherry on top, for some you even have to wait for specific dates (or change your system clock). A game this awful does not deserve to make these kinds of demands.

To try and find at least something positive to say: The levels do sometimes look pretty enough and do an admirable job of making things look like Minecraft. Regardless, anyone who enjoys Minecraft, good video games, fun, or life in general should stay as far away from this as humanly possible. You couldn't pay me to go through this torture again.

At the same time, I see negative reviews stating the game [i]does[/i] require you to always be online, even for Offline mode. That's possible – I didn't notice, because I am indeed always online.
Next comes character selection/creation. Rather than using Steam Cloud, or at least integrate well with the enforced Microsoft account login, you need to manually upload/download your character to back it up or use it across multiple devices. There is no automatic sync, and you'll find no end of forum posts where people seek clarification as to how this works, terrified of messing something up, or already having lost their progress. Even just the basic act of "picking the two characters who'll play local co-op together" gives you whiplash from the menu interactions and animations.

It doesn't get any better once you enter the actual game. Let's look at a tale of two maps – the in-level minimap, and the world map at the hub:

When you're in a level and need to see the minimap (you kinda have to if you don't want to miss areas you should explore), it is an overlay over the entire screen. The default playing experience is to hide the game behind a shadowy layer with a map outline, adding permanent visual noise to an already busy game. There's also a direction marker for your current objective, which is constantly near-invisible or literally blocked by the UI. On modern operating systems you can shake the mouse cursor and it briefly increases in size so you can spot it. In Dungeons I often moved my character around in large-ish circles so that I could more easily spot the direction marker as it shifted in relation to my movement.

When looking at the world map to determine your next level, you'll slowly learn that it doesn't matter. There is no structure, just chaos. You'll play every level dozens of times anyway – literally just the same crap, over and over again. Once that depressing fact settled in, I still hoped to gain [i]some[/i] information from the map – did we discover all the secrets in a level already? Is there any reason to pick a certain level next? You can figure this out – but even after understanding how to use it, the UI still always made me feel like a Boomer trying to navigate Snapchat.

It has been a month since I finished the game and I still have PTSD from interacting with the inventory system. If you're familiar with actual Minecraft, that is kinda hilarious in itself. For me, it boils down to the lack of a sorting option. You collect [b]a lot[/b] of trash while grinding. The inventory [i]groups[/i] things (armor, weapons, artifacts…), but you can't sort within those categories. Not even by a single criterium, let alone several helpful ones – power level, rarity, enchantment details. You have to manually arrange items, but that order will inevitably get messed up when you equip gear to your character, and items shuffle between equipped and inventory. It's a constant mess that you'll never be able to stay on top of.
To add insult to injury, this is a deliberate design choice. The game [i]does[/i] have sorting in one particular screen, the storage chest in your hub where excess items go. When interacting with that chest, you can sort in the way I suggested above. But moving things between the storage chest and your inventory is clunky and lacks multi-selection – so you get the same issue of progressively destroying your manual order. In rare occasions it may be beneficial to go to the storage chest and use  sorting there, but it's mostly useless and doesn't make the inventory system any less awful.

Enchanting and gifting items between characters isn't much better, but at least not bad enough to be worth as many words.

This may all sound like you spend most of your time in menues rather than exploring levels and fighting enemies, but that is not the case. Because the levels take [b]forever[/b]. Every single one of them is way too long and bloated. It's bad enough that you need to replay them so often, but it's also a 45+ minute commitment to start one. You can speedrun them, but then you don't level up or find the hidden paths of progression. I did 80% of the awful grind on my own while watching some TV show on the side, but me and my brother did most of the initial unlocking/xploring together in local co-op. During every single level we reached a point where we both groaned in desperation and exhaustion because it just would not freaking end.
If the game was actually fun to play, maybe we wouldn't even have noticed the length. But the combat is shallower than a puddle – just mindless, endless button mashing. No skill required, and the different weapons or armors don't make any meaningful difference. Even traversal is frustrating: You move too slowly, the maps are maze-like and the direction is often hard to see. At the same time there's loads of nooks and crannies where your character gets stuck. Even worse is that exploration is often useless with no rewards at the end of sidetracks – no chest, not even a bunch of enemies. Anyone remotely experienced in "game design language" would think has to be something there – but then you go and find ✨ nothing ✨. Putting it this way, I suppose you do find a good metaphor for the overall game.

Finally, the achievements are straight from hell. Imbalanced, half of them unlocking automatically as you play, the other half being somewhere on the spectrum between "laughably complex conditions that you need to look up, but actually easy to do" and "most insane grind of your life". As a cherry on top, for some you even have to wait for specific dates (or change your system clock). A game this awful does not deserve to make these kinds of demands.

To try and find at least something positive to say: The levels do sometimes look pretty enough and do an admirable job of making things look like Minecraft. Regardless, anyone who enjoys Minecraft, good video games, fun, or life in general should stay as far away from this as humanly possible. You couldn't pay me to go through this torture again.

Not even by a single criterium, let alone several helpful ones – power level, rarity, enchantment details. You have to manually arrange items, but that order will inevitably get messed up when you equip gear to your character, and items shuffle between equipped and inventory. It's a constant mess that you'll never be able to stay on top of.
To add insult to injury, this is a deliberate design choice. The game [i]does[/i] have sorting in one particular screen, the storage chest in your hub where excess items go. When interacting with that chest, you can sort in the way I suggested above. But moving things between the storage chest and your inventory is clunky and lacks multi-selection – so you get the same issue of progressively destroying your manual order. In rare occasions it may be beneficial to go to the storage chest and use  sorting there, but it's mostly useless and doesn't make the inventory system any less awful.

Enchanting and gifting items between characters isn't much better, but at least not bad enough to be worth as many words.

This may all sound like you spend most of your time in menues rather than exploring levels and fighting enemies, but that is not the case. Because the levels take [b]forever[/b]. Every single one of them is way too long and bloated. It's bad enough that you need to replay them so often, but it's also a 45+ minute commitment to start one. You can speedrun them, but then you don't level up or find the hidden paths of progression. I did 80% of the awful grind on my own while watching some TV show on the side, but me and my brother did most of the initial unlocking/xploring together in local co-op. During every single level we reached a point where we both groaned in desperation and exhaustion because it just would not freaking end.
If the game was actually fun to play, maybe we wouldn't even have noticed the length. But the combat is shallower than a puddle – just mindless, endless button mashing. No skill required, and the different weapons or armors don't make any meaningful difference. Even traversal is frustrating: You move too slowly, the maps are maze-like and the direction is often hard to see. At the same time there's loads of nooks and crannies where your character gets stuck. Even worse is that exploration is often useless with no rewards at the end of sidetracks – no chest, not even a bunch of enemies. Anyone remotely experienced in "game design language" would think has to be something there – but then you go and find ✨ nothing ✨. Putting it this way, I suppose you do find a good metaphor for the overall game.

Finally, the achievements are straight from hell. Imbalanced, half of them unlocking automatically as you play, the other half being somewhere on the spectrum between "laughably complex conditions that you need to look up, but actually easy to do" and "most insane grind of your life". As a cherry on top, for some you even have to wait for specific dates (or change your system clock). A game this awful does not deserve to make these kinds of demands.

To try and find at least something positive to say: The levels do sometimes look pretty enough and do an admirable job of making things look like Minecraft. Regardless, anyone who enjoys Minecraft, good video games, fun, or life in general should stay as far away from this as humanly possible. You couldn't pay me to go through this torture again.

translations.english:
I don't even know where to begin to describe how much I [i]loathe[/i] this game. I love Minecraft – it's my most played game of all time, thousands of hours with no end in sight. So I had a lot of love ready for any worthy expansion to the wonderful world of mining and crafting.

Suffering through this miserable experience seems to have taught me that I don't like dungeon crawler RPGs. I played some [i]Diablo 2[/i] when it was released, but I was too young to properly engage with a game like that back then and I don't think I ever played anything similar. Which I intend to keep that way now, because I never want to experience such boring, mindless, repetitive garbage again. Doing my taxes is more engaging than playing the same map fifty times to level up my character – only for that to not change a single thing about the gameplay experience.

Even if you do enjoy the genre I still think Minecraft Dungeons is uniquely awful. First off, the story might as well not exist. There is maybe 20 sentences total throughout a couple of cut-scenes in a game that asks for 100+ hours of playtime. No cohesion, no real progression, and worst of all nothing that you emotionally connect with. The UI is a catastrophe. No person guilty for creating it should be allowed near a computer again. I'd rather update my Mac to Liquid Glass than to having to engage with any UI elements of this game again.

The start menu already is a mess – you must choose between Online and Offline mode before entering the game. I have 100%ed this game and still do not really understand the difference. I first assumed I had to pick Online so my progression would count, but that's not the case. After realizing that, I always picked Offline and everything worked exactly as before. The season pass system with daily/weekly challenges, the Tower game mode (which is on a global schedule), playing co-op… none of the things that I expected to require Online actually did. At the same time, I see negative reviews stating the game [i]does[/i] require you to always be online, even for Offline mode. That's possible – I didn't notice, because I am indeed always online.
Next comes character selection/creation. Rather than using Steam Cloud, or at least integrate well with the enforced Microsoft account login, you need to manually upload/download your character to back it up or use it across multiple devices. There is no automatic sync, and you'll find no end of forum posts where people seek clarification as to how this works, terrified of messing something up, or already having lost their progress. Even just the basic act of "picking the two characters who'll play local co-op together" gives you whiplash from the menu interactions and animations.

It doesn't get any better once you enter the actual game. Let's look at a tale of two maps – the in-level minimap, and the world map at the hub:

When you're in a level and need to see the minimap (you kinda have to if you don't want to miss areas you should explore), it is an overlay over the entire screen. The default playing experience is to hide the game behind a shadowy layer with a map outline, adding permanent visual noise to an already busy game. There's also a direction marker for your current objective, which is constantly near-invisible or literally blocked by the UI. On modern operating systems you can shake the mouse cursor and it briefly increases in size so you can spot it. In Dungeons I often moved my character around in large-ish circles so that I could more easily spot the direction marker as it shifted in relation to my movement.

When looking at the world map to determine your next level, you'll slowly learn that it doesn't matter. There is no structure, just chaos. You'll play every level dozens of times anyway – literally just the same crap, over and over again. Once that depressing fact settled in, I still hoped to gain [i]some[/i] information from the map – did we discover all the secrets in a level already? Is there any reason to pick a certain level next? You can figure this out – but even after understanding how to use it, the UI still always made me feel like a Boomer trying to navigate Snapchat.

It has been a month since I finished the game and I still have PTSD from interacting with the inventory system. If you're familiar with actual Minecraft, that is kinda hilarious in itself. For me, it boils down to the lack of a sorting option. You collect [b]a lot[/b] of trash while grinding. The inventory [i]groups[/i] things (armor, weapons, artifacts…), but you can't sort within those categories. Not even by a single criterium, let alone several helpful ones – power level, rarity, enchantment details. You have to manually arrange items, but that order will inevitably get messed up when you equip gear to your character, and items shuffle between equipped and inventory. It's a constant mess that you'll never be able to stay on top of.
To add insult to injury, this is a deliberate design choice. The game [i]does[/i] have sorting in one particular screen, the storage chest in your hub where excess items go. When interacting with that chest, you can sort in the way I suggested above. But moving things between the storage chest and your inventory is clunky and lacks multi-selection – so you get the same issue of progressively destroying your manual order. In rare occasions it may be beneficial to go to the storage chest and use  sorting there, but it's mostly useless and doesn't make the inventory system any less awful.

Enchanting and gifting items between characters isn't much better, but at least not bad enough to be worth as many words.

This may all sound like you spend most of your time in menues rather than exploring levels and fighting enemies, but that is not the case. Because the levels take [b]forever[/b]. Every single one of them is way too long and bloated. It's bad enough that you need to replay them so often, but it's also a 45+ minute commitment to start one. You can speedrun them, but then you don't level up or find the hidden paths of progression. I did 80% of the awful grind on my own while watching some TV show on the side, but me and my brother did most of the initial unlocking/xploring together in local co-op. During every single level we reached a point where we both groaned in desperation and exhaustion because it just would not freaking end.
If the game was actually fun to play, maybe we wouldn't even have noticed the length. But the combat is shallower than a puddle – just mindless, endless button mashing. No skill required, and the different weapons or armors don't make any meaningful difference. Even traversal is frustrating: You move too slowly, the maps are maze-like and the direction is often hard to see. At the same time there's loads of nooks and crannies where your character gets stuck. Even worse is that exploration is often useless with no rewards at the end of sidetracks – no chest, not even a bunch of enemies. Anyone remotely experienced in "game design language" would think has to be something there – but then you go and find ✨ nothing ✨. Putting it this way, I suppose you do find a good metaphor for the overall game.

Finally, the achievements are straight from hell. Imbalanced, half of them unlocking automatically as you play, the other half being somewhere on the spectrum between "laughably complex conditions that you need to look up, but actually easy to do" and "most insane grind of your life". Regardless, anyone who enjoys Minecraft, good video games, fun, or life in general should stay as far away from this as humanly possible. You couldn't pay me to go through this torture again.

At the same time, I see negative reviews stating the game [i]does[/i] require you to always be online, even for Offline mode. That's possible – I didn't notice, because I am indeed always online.
Next comes character selection/creation. Rather than using Steam Cloud, or at least integrate well with the enforced Microsoft account login, you need to manually upload/download your character to back it up or use it across multiple devices. There is no automatic sync, and you'll find no end of forum posts where people seek clarification as to how this works, terrified of messing something up, or already having lost their progress. Even just the basic act of "picking the two characters who'll play local co-op together" gives you whiplash from the menu interactions and animations.

It doesn't get any better once you enter the actual game. Let's look at a tale of two maps – the in-level minimap, and the world map at the hub:

When you're in a level and need to see the minimap (you kinda have to if you don't want to miss areas you should explore), it is an overlay over the entire screen. The default playing experience is to hide the game behind a shadowy layer with a map outline, adding permanent visual noise to an already busy game. There's also a direction marker for your current objective, which is constantly near-invisible or literally blocked by the UI. On modern operating systems you can shake the mouse cursor and it briefly increases in size so you can spot it. In Dungeons I often moved my character around in large-ish circles so that I could more easily spot the direction marker as it shifted in relation to my movement.

When looking at the world map to determine your next level, you'll slowly learn that it doesn't matter. There is no structure, just chaos. You'll play every level dozens of times anyway – literally just the same crap, over and over again. Once that depressing fact settled in, I still hoped to gain [i]some[/i] information from the map – did we discover all the secrets in a level already? Is there any reason to pick a certain level next? You can figure this out – but even after understanding how to use it, the UI still always made me feel like a Boomer trying to navigate Snapchat.

It has been a month since I finished the game and I still have PTSD from interacting with the inventory system. If you're familiar with actual Minecraft, that is kinda hilarious in itself. For me, it boils down to the lack of a sorting option. You collect [b]a lot[/b] of trash while grinding. The inventory [i]groups[/i] things (armor, weapons, artifacts…), but you can't sort within those categories. Not even by a single criterium, let alone several helpful ones – power level, rarity, enchantment details. You have to manually arrange items, but that order will inevitably get messed up when you equip gear to your character, and items shuffle between equipped and inventory. It's a constant mess that you'll never be able to stay on top of.
To add insult to injury, this is a deliberate design choice. The game [i]does[/i] have sorting in one particular screen, the storage chest in your hub where excess items go. When interacting with that chest, you can sort in the way I suggested above. But moving things between the storage chest and your inventory is clunky and lacks multi-selection – so you get the same issue of progressively destroying your manual order. In rare occasions it may be beneficial to go to the storage chest and use  sorting there, but it's mostly useless and doesn't make the inventory system any less awful.

Enchanting and gifting items between characters isn't much better, but at least not bad enough to be worth as many words.

This may all sound like you spend most of your time in menues rather than exploring levels and fighting enemies, but that is not the case. Because the levels take [b]forever[/b]. Every single one of them is way too long and bloated. It's bad enough that you need to replay them so often, but it's also a 45+ minute commitment to start one. You can speedrun them, but then you don't level up or find the hidden paths of progression. I did 80% of the awful grind on my own while watching some TV show on the side, but me and my brother did most of the initial unlocking/xploring together in local co-op. During every single level we reached a point where we both groaned in desperation and exhaustion because it just would not freaking end.
If the game was actually fun to play, maybe we wouldn't even have noticed the length. But the combat is shallower than a puddle – just mindless, endless button mashing. No skill required, and the different weapons or armors don't make any meaningful difference. Even traversal is frustrating: You move too slowly, the maps are maze-like and the direction is often hard to see. At the same time there's loads of nooks and crannies where your character gets stuck. Even worse is that exploration is often useless with no rewards at the end of sidetracks – no chest, not even a bunch of enemies. Anyone remotely experienced in "game design language" would think has to be something there – but then you go and find ✨ nothing ✨. Putting it this way, I suppose you do find a good metaphor for the overall game.

Finally, the achievements are straight from hell. Imbalanced, half of them unlocking automatically as you play, the other half being somewhere on the spectrum between "laughably complex conditions that you need to look up, but actually easy to do" and "most insane grind of your life". As a cherry on top, for some you even have to wait for specific dates (or change your system clock). A game this awful does not deserve to make these kinds of demands.

To try and find at least something positive to say: The levels do sometimes look pretty enough and do an admirable job of making things look like Minecraft. Regardless, anyone who enjoys Minecraft, good video games, fun, or life in general should stay as far away from this as humanly possible. You couldn't pay me to go through this torture again.

negative.original:
I did not enjoy this. It was frustrating every step of the way. After around two hours of playing all I could think was: I could be playing [i]Path of Exiles 2[/i] instead. I beat the main map and tried out all the game modes, but did not this worth the grind to partake in endgame max level super hard scaling content. 

That said, this is a very accessible introduction to ARPGs, especially for younger players and  Minecraft fans. I am no longer part of that target audience, but 13 year old me would have loved it.

[h3] Things I did not like [/h3]
[list]
[*] Mouse and Keyboard design. This uses mouse movement which is not totally unheard of but was clearly not the intended game design. Moving between attacks is a core part of combat, but it is difficult using mouse clicks that also control attacking based on enemies under cursor. Controller does not have this issue.
[*] A significant amount of the core game is behind DLCs (That I will not be buying after beating the base game). The best way I could describe it is that base game is stage 1 and game modes, then stages 2-4 are DLC. This should just be a single more expensive game that is complete instead of segmented.
[*] You must use a Microsoft account with xbox profile to play at all.
[*] It is live service to minecraft servers which I have found to be unreliable. It often does not connect, I disconnected at least once every time I tried to play. You can still play, but quite a few features will not work. If it goes out during a run, it may also kick you back to the home screen voiding everything you got in that run.
[/list]

[h3] Things I am mixed on [/h3]
[list]
[*] Adventure pass (battle pass thing), this did not need any more monetization.
[*] It is balanced for multiplayer. I did it solo. I managed, but it was actively frustrating at times. (pets are great distractions, also chose harder than recommended threat because it is not that hard)
[*] The endless loot treadmill. I know that is part of the diablo DNA but I despise it. The Implementation in this game was not terrible, but I still do not enjoy it. 
[*] The enchantment system. Being a gear based system, the enchantment system offers modifiers that act much like nodes in a skill tree. In fact, you actually get the enchantment points from leveling up like skill points in other games. This means that you must find a weapon that is both the type you want and with the enchantments you want. This system can be blamed as a reason the loot treadmill is endless. A simple skill tree with enchantments as nodes would have worked just as well and cut grind time considerably.
[/list]

[h3] Things I liked [/h3]
[list]
[*] The upgrade system. Gear from the start can be upgraded and used at the end if you want.
[*] The different game modes. Just the primary story maps would get old really really fast. The tower is more my kind of game.
[/list]

I did not enjoy this. It was frustrating every step of the way. After around two hours of playing all I could think was: I could be playing [i]Path of Exiles 2[/i] instead. I beat the main map and tried out all the game modes, but did not this worth the grind to partake in endgame max level super hard scaling content. 

That said, this is a very accessible introduction to ARPGs, especially for younger players and  Minecraft fans. I am no longer part of that target audience, but 13 year old me would have loved it.

[h3] Things I did not like [/h3]
[list]
[*] Mouse and Keyboard design. This uses mouse movement which is not totally unheard of but was clearly not the intended game design. Moving between attacks is a core part of combat, but it is difficult using mouse clicks that also control attacking based on enemies under cursor. Controller does not have this issue.
[*] A significant amount of the core game is behind DLCs (That I will not be buying after beating the base game). The best way I could describe it is that base game is stage 1 and game modes, then stages 2-4 are DLC. This should just be a single more expensive game that is complete instead of segmented.
[*] You must use a Microsoft account with xbox profile to play at all.
[*] It is live service to minecraft servers which I have found to be unreliable. It often does not connect, I disconnected at least once every time I tried to play. You can still play, but quite a few features will not work. If it goes out during a run, it may also kick you back to the home screen voiding everything you got in that run.
[/list]

[h3] Things I am mixed on [/h3]
[list]
[*] Adventure pass (battle pass thing), this did not need any more monetization.
[*] It is balanced for multiplayer. I did it solo. I managed, but it was actively frustrating at times. (pets are great distractions, also chose harder than recommended threat because it is not that hard)
[*] The endless loot treadmill. I know that is part of the diablo DNA but I despise it. The Implementation in this game was not terrible, but I still do not enjoy it. 
[*] The enchantment system. Being a gear based system, the enchantment system offers modifiers that act much like nodes in a skill tree. In fact, you actually get the enchantment points from leveling up like skill points in other games. This means that you must find a weapon that is both the type you want and with the enchantments you want. This system can be blamed as a reason the loot treadmill is endless. A simple skill tree with enchantments as nodes would have worked just as well and cut grind time considerably.
[/list]

[h3] Things I liked [/h3]
[list]
[*] The upgrade system. Gear from the start can be upgraded and used at the end if you want.
[*] The different game modes. Just the primary story maps would get old really really fast. The tower is more my kind of game.
[/list]

Also unplayable on ultrawide without external mods.

negative.original: This game is utter garbage and no balance to it creating a BS level of challenge that unless you have a full party is just not fun. Enemies do far too much damage, potion cooldown is far too long, combat is janky and not good, no blocking, etc and just makes for an overall bad experience. I'll go back to playing PoE2 and other games that are actually fun.
